clue.text: Handy weapon for art-master's employer

parts.note: MA is the abbreviation for Master of Arts, a degree holder in the arts
one who employs or makes use of something is a user

explanation.surface: A gun that would suit whoever employs the drawing teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Art-master' reads as a painting teacher, but it is MA, Master of Arts. The 's is no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mauser is a German make of pistol and rifle, a weapon carried in the hand.

clue.text: Notwithstanding there's a high tone to the joint

parts.note: alt is a musical term for a high note, as in 'in alt'
hough is the hock, the joint in an animal's hind leg

explanation.surface: Despite everything, the cut of meat has an elevated flavour.
explanation.walkthrough: HOUGH (pronounced 'hock') is a Scottish word for that joint and its meat.
explanation.definitionFit: Although and notwithstanding both introduce a concession, meaning 'in spite of the fact'.

clue.text: Wide-eyed, about five are on the no-calorie diet

indicators.note: about means the staring word goes round the numeral

parts.note: wide-eyed means staring
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: Five dieters on a strict regime look on with wide eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts V inside STARING.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone eating nothing at all, taking in no energy from food, is going hungry.

clue.text: Caged cause of Blake's heavenly rage

definitions.text: Caged cause of Blake's heavenly rage

parts.words: Caged cause of Blake's heavenly rage
parts.note: William Blake's Auguries of Innocence: 'A Robin ___ in a Cage / Puts all Heaven in a Rage', the missing word being the bird's name

explanation.surface: What was locked up that made heaven furious in Blake's poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from William Blake's Auguries of Innocence.
explanation.definitionFit: Blake's caged robin is named by its red-feathered chest, an old name for the bird.

clue.text: St Bernard might let you in

definitions.text: St Bernard might let you in

parts.words: St Bernard might let you in
parts.note: the St Bernard is not the rescue dog but the Great St Bernard, an Alpine pass; a secret word of entry, a pass's 'word', gets you past a sentry

explanation.surface: A rescue dog on the mountain could open the door for you.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog of the surface is a red herring: the Great St Bernard is a pass through the Alps.
explanation.definitionFit: A secret term spoken to a guard grants entry, as a mountain pass grants passage.

clue.text: The first thing attracting interest in company

definitions.text: The first thing attracting interest in company

parts.words: The first thing attracting interest in company
parts.note: sounds like what catches attention at a party, but means a stake in a firm that is paid its dividend before ordinary holdings

explanation.surface: What first catches the eye when you are out among other people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interest' is the return paid on an investment, and 'company' a business firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Holders of this kind of stock are entitled to their dividend ahead of ordinary shareholders.

clue.text: Stand by to take wine

parts.note: to sup is to take a drink or food in small mouthfuls
port is a fortified wine from Portugal

explanation.surface: A waiter is told to wait ready to pour the wine.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand by someone is to back them up.

clue.text: The rate's higher when you change ends

definitions.text: The rate's higher when you change ends

parts.words: The rate's higher when you change ends
parts.note: describes extra time in a match, when teams switch ends, and also hours beyond the normal working day, paid at a higher rate

explanation.surface: A remark about scoring rising after half-time.
explanation.walkthrough: Two pictures overlap: the higher pay for extra hours and the extra period of a match.
explanation.definitionFit: Work beyond normal hours is paid at an enhanced rate, and a match's extra period follows a change of ends.

clue.text: I'd back Sir Patrick on the point, or go without

indicators.note: back means the letters for I'd are read in reverse

parts.note: Sir Patrick Spens is the hero of a famous Scottish ballad
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Someone supports a knight on a matter of detail, or else does without.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns ID into DI. Sir Patrick Spens drowns at sea in an old Scots ballad.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispense with something is to do without it.

clue.text: Bracket with colossal stand

definitions.meaning: in gunnery, to bracket a target is to land shots on either side of it
the Colossus of Rhodes was said to stand with one foot on each side of the harbour mouth

explanation.surface: A shelf bracket attached to a gigantic stand.
explanation.definitionFit: Shots falling on both sides of a target, or legs planted either side of something, both span it.

clue.text: A meal, first to last, of bits of shoe-leather

indicators.note: the opening letter of the meal word is taken from the front and sent to the back

parts.note: supper is an evening meal

explanation.surface: A meal made of scraps of boot leather, a hungry cobbler's dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first to last' moves the S of SUPPER to its end, giving UPPERS.
explanation.definitionFit: The uppers of a shoe are the leather parts above the sole.

clue.text: Come to the point — leave padre to turn in.

indicators.note: in tells you the turned piece sits inside the word for leave

parts.note: a congé is formal leave or permission to depart

indicators.note: to turn tells you to read the clergyman's abbreviation backwards

parts.note: a padre is a clergyman, abbreviated Rev for Reverend

explanation.surface: A request to let the chaplain go to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to turn' makes VER from REV, and 'in' puts it inside CONGE. 'Leave' looks like a verb but is the noun congé.
explanation.definitionFit: Lines that converge meet at a single place, coming together at a point.

clue.text: It holds one up by the neck

definitions.text: It holds one up by the neck

parts.words: It holds one up by the neck
parts.note: sounds like a garrotter or a hangman, but describes a glass vessel for drink, which is gripped at its narrow top

explanation.surface: A threat of violence: something grabs you by the throat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a mugging; a wine container is lifted by its neck.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass container for liquids has a narrow neck by which it is usually held.

clue.text: Foreign area not far from seat of trouble

parts.note: not far means near

indicators.note: trouble suggests disorder, so the letters of seat are jumbled

explanation.surface: A troubled overseas region close to the centre of conflict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of trouble' rearranges SEAT into EAST.
explanation.definitionFit: The Near East is an old term for the lands of the eastern Mediterranean, a region abroad.

clue.text: Huge wins in egg-yield perhaps

indicators.note: a yield here is the output of shuffling, signalling that the letters given are rearranged

explanation.surface: Bumper gains in a poultry farm's egg production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'yield perhaps' rearranges WINS, IN and EGG into SWINGEING.
explanation.definitionFit: Swingeing, a British word, means severe or very large, as in swingeing cuts.

clue.text: Smoked seabird

definitions.meaning: a coarse cut tobacco, the thing smoked

explanation.surface: A seabird that has been cured in smoke.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong shredded pipe tobacco shares its name with a cormorant of rocky coasts.

clue.text: Bad sailor's opinion supports Botticelli's Venus

definitions.meaning: a poor sailor thinks the sea is hell
in Botticelli's Birth of Venus the goddess stands on a scallop

explanation.surface: A seasick sailor's view that holds up a famous painting.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer split as SEA'S HELL for the first sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A seasick sailor would call the ocean torment; Botticelli painted Venus standing on a scallop.

clue.text: Unqualified if not unrivalled on the stage

definitions.text: if not unrivalled on the stage
definitions.meaning: Captain Jack, a character in Sheridan's play The Rivals, so not without rivals

explanation.surface: An unqualified actor who still has no equal in the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: In Sheridan's comedy The Rivals, Captain Absolute is one of the rivals, hence 'not unrivalled'.
explanation.definitionFit: Absolute means complete and unconditional; it is also the surname of Sheridan's rival suitor.

clue.text: Dried up before the end, after opening of speech

indicators.note: after puts the letters for before behind the opening letter
the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: ere is an old word for before; 'the end' places it at the end of the answer

explanation.surface: A throat dried up before the speech finished, just after it began.
explanation.walkthrough: Take S, the first letter of 'speech', then ERE (before).
explanation.definitionFit: Sere is a literary word for withered or parched, as of autumn leaves.

clue.text: He insists that a sportsman leaves the fish, right ?

indicators.note: leaves means the player's word departs from the fish's name

parts.note: the stickleback is a small spiny freshwater fish
a back is a defensive player in football or hockey

explanation.surface: Someone says a footballer should leave the fish alone, and rightly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' takes BACK out of STICKLEBACK, leaving STICKLE, then add R.
explanation.definitionFit: A stickler is a person who insists on exactness.

clue.text: Transports faulty parts on both sides of the river

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit on either side of the river's name
faulty suggests something wrong, so the letters of parts are put in another order

parts.note: the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Defective components carried on either bank of a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'faulty' rearranges PARTS into RAPTS, and 'on both sides of' wraps those letters round URE.
explanation.definitionFit: Raptures and transports are both states of overwhelming delight.

clue.text: He should have something in store for us

definitions.text: He should have something in store for us

parts.words: He should have something in store for us
parts.note: sounds like a promise of a future treat, but means a trader who keeps goods in his shop for customers

explanation.surface: Someone is planning a surprise for us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In store' here means held in a shop, not lying ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: A retailer who keeps a particular line of goods available to buy is said to carry them.

clue.text: Extend gaol-sentence

definitions.meaning: to extend is to lengthen or pull out
slang for a term in prison

explanation.surface: A prisoner's term is lengthened.
explanation.definitionFit: To lengthen something is to pull it out further, and a spell in prison is slang for a period served.

clue.text: " When swift Camilla —— the plain " (Pope)

parts.note: a gap-fill from Alexander Pope's Essay on Criticism: 'When swift Camilla ___ the plain', the missing verb meaning sweeps swiftly across

explanation.walkthrough: The dash in the printed clue marks the missing word. Camilla is the swift-footed warrior maiden of Virgil's Aeneid.
explanation.definitionFit: Pope's line has Camilla racing over the ground; to range quickly over an area is to sweep it.

clue.text: The London of the Forsytes or their shrewdness?

parts.note: The Forsyte Saga is John Galsworthy's series of novels about the Forsyte family
London's financial district is the City, the Forsytes' world of money

explanation.surface: Galsworthy's London, or the canny business sense of his characters.
explanation.walkthrough: The Forsytes are a family of London businessmen; their book is a saga, and their London the City.
explanation.definitionFit: Sagacity is wisdom and keen judgement, the quality of being astute.

clue.text: Rejoices in the reformation of a former slut

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: a reformation reshapes something, so the letters of slut are reordered

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted that a fallen woman has mended her ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reformation of' rearranges SLUT into ULTS, after EX.
explanation.definitionFit: To exult is to show triumphant joy.

clue.text: A team all returning by railway at a branch-junction

parts.note: a cricket or football team is an eleven, XI in Roman numerals

indicators.note: returning means the word all is read backwards

explanation.surface: A whole side travelling home by train, changing at a junction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns ALL into LLA. In botany the axil is the angle where a leaf or branch joins the stem.
explanation.definitionFit: Axillary means growing in the angle where a branch meets its stem.

clue.text: But a Windward Island must have one such coast?

definitions.text: But a Windward Island must have one such coast?

parts.words: But a Windward Island must have one such coast?
parts.note: an island facing the wind on one side must have a sheltered side away from it, the side sailors fear when the wind blows onto it

explanation.surface: A question about the shoreline of a Caribbean island.
explanation.walkthrough: The Windward Islands are in the Caribbean; any island, however windward, has a downwind shore.
explanation.definitionFit: A coast the wind blows towards is one on to which a ship may be driven, the sheltered side being the island's downwind face.

clue.text: Gaudy, or somewhat fishy ?

parts.note: the word fishy is read as a fish, the gar, followed by a suffix
the suffix -ish means somewhat, as in reddish

explanation.surface: Is something gaudy, or a bit suspicious?
explanation.walkthrough: 'fishy' is split as fish plus -y; swap in the gar (a long-snouted fish) and the suffix -ish for 'somewhat'.
explanation.definitionFit: Garish describes colours that are loud and showy.
